Master of Arts in International Relations Admission requirements: undergraduate credit in political science or related discipline; current scores from the GRE, GMAT, or MAT are required for applicants with a cumulative undergraduate GPA below 3.0 Program requirements: a minimum of 30 credits including 9 credits in required core courses and 9 credits in concentration courses.

For a concentration in global peace studies, select three courses from PSY 478, PSY 690, PSC 546, PSC 551, PSC 555, PSC 556, PSC 586, PSC 581 and PSC 582 and PSC 588.
Courses can be applied to only one concentration.
Students can apply no more than two special topics seminars (PSC 581/PSC582) to fulfill their concentration requirements.
Thesis and nonthesis options.
Nonthesis option requires one course with a substantial paper requirement that involves significant independent research and a comprehensive examination with written and oral components.
Master of Public Administration (M.P.A.) The Master of Public Administration (M.P.A.) Program leads to the M.P.A. degree conferred by the University of Rhode Island.

This program is offered in an accelerated online format and provides federal, state, city, and nonprofit officials and agencies with flexible access to its instructional programs and research expertise.
In addition to delivering its online degree and certificate programs, internships, and workshops, the M.P.A. faculty conducts research into the formation and implementation of public policy and the administration of public and nonprofit agencies.
Admission requirements: Minimum GPA of 2.5.
Program requirements: a minimum of 36 credits, including completion of the Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy, 12 credits through the completion of either the Public Management certificate or the Policy Analysis certificate, and 12 elective credits.
The 3 required core courses of the Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy are PSC 501, PSC 502, and PSC 504.
Students completing this certificate can choose an additional 3 credits from either PSC 508, PSC 556, PSC 590, or PSC 592.
For a certificate in Public Management, students must complete 12 credits from the following courses: PSC 503, PSC 506, PSC 507, PSC 508, PSC 556, PSC 573, or PSC 592.

For a certificate in Policy Analysis, students must complete 12 credits from the following courses: PSC 505, PSC 508, PSC 524, PSC 556, PSC 583, PSC 510, or PSC 592.
Students graduating from the

4 M.P.A. program are required to complete the PSC 592 capstone course, which can only be applied toward one of the M.P.A. certificate programs.
PSC 508, PSC 555, and PSC 556 can only be applied to one of the M.P.A. certificate programs.
Students in the MPA program taking elective courses at other institutions will be governed by the same regulations effective for courses taken at URI.
Under this rule, grades (including failures) for all graduate courses taken at other institutions will be included in the grade point average and will become part of the student’s record.
The Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy, the Public Management certificate, and the Policy Analysis certificate offered by the MPA program can also be completed as independent, standalone certificate programs.
Each certificate program requires at least 12 credits.
Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy A 12-credit post-baccalaureate Professional Certificate in Public Administration and Policy is open to current students and college graduates with or without the M.P.A. degree.

This core certificate introduces students to concepts that are crucial for success in public and non-profit professional settings related to public administration and policy, including diversity and inclusion, writing for grant and policy audiences, ethics, and the historical evolution of the public administration and policy fields.
Completion of the following courses is required: PSC 501, Seminar in Public Administration and Policy; PSC 502, Diversity and Inclusion in Public Administration and Policy; and PSC 504, Ethics in Public Administration and Policy.
The remaining 3 credits can be chosen from the following courses: PSC 508, Policy and Grant Writing; PSC 555, Directed Study; PSC 556, Directed Study; PSC 590, Internship in Public Administration and Policy; PSC 592, Capstone in Public Administration and Policy.
Public Management Certificate A 12-credit post-baccalaureate Public Management Certificate is open to all current students and college graduates with or without the M.P.A. degree.

Students completing a certificate in Public Management will be competitive applicants for public or non-profit positions requiring financial and budgetary expertise, leadership skills, knowledge of administrative law and procedure, and the

5 management of agency personnel.
Completion of this certificate is contingent on having earned at least 12 credits in the following courses: PSC 503, Problems in Public Personnel Administration; PSC 506, Seminar in Budgetary Politics; PSC 507, Public Finance; PSC 508, Policy and Grant Writing; PSC 555, Directed Study; PSC 556, Directed Study; PSC 573, Administrative Law; PSC 592, Capstone in Public Administration and Policy.
Policy Analysis Certificate A 12-credit post-baccalaureate Policy Analysis Certificate is open to current students and college graduates with or without the M.P.A. degree.
Students completing the Policy Analysis certificate will develop research and analytical capabilities that will allow them to become effective at shaping public policy either within public agencies, nonprofit agencies, or as part of a broader policymaking process.

Completion of this certificate is contingent on having earned at least 12 credits in the following courses: PSC 505, Public Program Evaluation; PSC 508 Policy and Grant Writing; PSC 510 Critical Topics in Public Policy; PSC 524, Seminar in Public Policy Problems; PSC 555, Directed Study; PSC 556, Directed Study; PSC 583, Public Policy Analysis; PSC 592, Capstone in Public Administration and Policy.
MPA and MLIS Cooperative Program A cooperative program permits joint enrollment in URI’s Master of Public Administration and Master of Library and Information Studies programs.
The integrated pursuit of the two degrees makes it possible for six credits of appropriately selected coursework from one program to serve as electives in the other, and for six credits of such coursework to be applied in the opposite direction.
Thus, when planned and taken jointly, the two programs can be completed with a total of 60 credits.
Admission requirements: GRE and other requirements listed for MPA and MLIS.
Applicants must apply and be accepted in both programs.
Applications to both programs must indicate MPA/MLIS as the field of specialization.

Program requirements: each student must complete the required core courses for both programs plus three credits of PSC 590 for the MPA.
After consultation with,

6 and approval of, both departments, students must file separate programs of study for each degree, indicating the courses to be jointly counted. Each student must pass the separate comprehensive examination for each degree. A student who fails to complete one of the programs may, of course, complete the other in accordance with the separate program of study. Accelerated Bachelor’s to Master’s Degrees International Studies B.A. to International Relations Master’s degree Political Science B.A. to International Relations Master’s degree Students in the International Studies B.A. and the Political Science B.A. programs are eligible to apply for an Accelerated Bachelor’s to Master’s Degree (IRABM) program to earn a Master’s in International Relations. All courses required by the International Studies B.A. and the Political Science B.A. and the International Relations Master’s are required. Additional requirements for the IRABM program are listed below. Prerequisites: Prior to application, students must receive a B or better in PSC 210 or PSC 211, or equivalent courses at the discretion of the department. Applying for the IRABM: To apply for the IRABM program, students must have earned a minimum of 75 credits and have a 3.0 GPA. Students will be enrolled in the IRABM program only after they have met the Graduate School admission requirements and have completed 90 undergraduate credits. See International Relations ABM in the ABM section of this catalog for additional information. 7. Signature of the President

Summary description of the proposed organizational change Film/Media (FLM) became a BA degree program in AY 2006, after existing as an interdepartmental minor (Film Studies) since AY 1999. FLM remains one of the unique interdisciplinary majors (and minors) at URI, with courses that count towards the major

2 spanning 14 different disciplines across the University.
Film/Media has been a unit in the Harrington School of Communication and Media since the inception of the Harrington School in 2008.
The program offers hands-on, technical experience and professional preparation in documentary, experimental, narrative, commercial, and new and evolving media production, balanced with an emphasis on the study of international cinemas, film and media history, criticism, and theory.
This curriculum has allowed for FLM to be a focal point for delivery of University and Harrington School goals, as reflected in their strategic plans, with an emphasis on enhancing international and diverse cultural awareness and relationships, offering experiential and collaborative learning, preparation for successful professional careers, and exposure to interdisciplinary disciplines that emphasize innovative and integrative critical thinking.
Departmental status will situate FLM in a stronger competitive position to attract prospective students to the Harrington School and the future success and commitment to communications and media that the School promises.

FLM has long been a discipline that attracts potential University applicants, and it is necessary that we present a quality, fully formed department that enhances the entire Harrington School project and URI.
Departmental status will underscore and enhance our national and global reputation: it is essential for our faculty to place FLM in a more competitive position to attract internal and external funding and grant opportunities, as well as encouraging internship and experiential opportunities for our students, and career advancement for our growing number of alumni.
Departmental status for Film/Media will emphasize the University’s commitment to offering our students the necessary tools and technologies that will shape their futures.
This proposal for departmental status for Film/Media is based on its past growth, the intense relevance and importance of visual culture and its production as a core skill for meeting the future of communications across media and industry, the continued development of curriculum that expands the majors’ goals and outcomes, and which are supported by a solid infrastructure which exceeds what is available with program status.

FLM must be confirmed as a department because the designation is essential to create this infrastructure to underscore its relevance to our students and to deliver the curriculum that will support not only this major, but the broader inter-departmental goals and core values of the Harrington School and the University.
It should be emphasized that the global Film/TV industry in 2020 was estimated to be valued at $244.4 billion, with Berkshire Hathaway estimating that this will reach $284 billion

3 by 2023.*1 Our Film/Media major, which is designed to promote student creativity as well as the attainment of essential professional technical skills, prepares our students for the widest variety of jobs in these industries, as well as the jobs of the future which they will be able to successfully negotiate with the skills and flexibility they develop in the Film/Media major.
For our majors to successfully train in and prepare for participation in this complex, lucrative, and essential industry, which sits at the forefront of 21st century media and creative innovation, the recognition and advantages of situating Film/Media equally among departments at URI is necessary and will help to assure that we attract and retain students in this major--as well as securing the importance of FLM to potential external mentors for our majors and potential donors to the Harington School and the University. 8.

RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change. 1.
Explain why the organizational change is being proposed.
Film/Media originally emerged as an outgrowth of URI’s English Department and became a major in the College of Arts and Sciences in the 2006 academic year.
It had existed as an Interdepartmental Minor (Film Studies) since at least 1998, and the smaller number of majors at the time of its inception as a major did not, perhaps, seem to warrant immediate 1 Business Wire, 8 August 2020. https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20200821005370/en/Global-Film-and-Video- Market-Report-2020-to-2030---COVID-19-Impact-and-Recovery---ResearchAndMarkets.com

4 department status.
As we have reached 15 years of the growth and impact of the Film/Media major, it is now of importance to finally address this issue.
Film/Media has long functioned as a department, without being awarded Departmental status.
FLM operates as a fully-fledged university department and is expected to fulfill the demands, expectations, and duties of an academic unit at that level: Film/Media has its own budget--and in addition to the budget afforded to us from the College of Arts & Sciences and the University, we manage approximately $125,000 in lab fees annually which are used to purchase and repair equipment, hardware and software, and to meet the financial demands that are necessary to adequately deliver courses and classrooms for the major.
Film/Media’s director fulfills all of the obligations and responsibilities of a department chair, and our faculty--tenure-track, full-time, Joint, and PTF--who exemplify dedicated and engaged pedagogical and scholarly rigor-- do not benefit from being identified or recognized as members of a valued academic department and discipline in the University.

Film/Media recorded 236 majors in Oct. 2020 and is the 5th largest major in Arts & Sciences, and the 2nd largest in the Harrington School.
The major has grown by 43% in the 5 years since 2017.
The program has served as a flagship for the Harrington School and the University in attracting prospective students, and, for the most part, the number of our incoming Freshmen class has grown steadily over the years from 28 in AY 2007 to an entering class of 48 in September 2020.
It should be noted that in the four B.A.-granting undergraduate majors that comprise the Harrington School, all except FLM operate with departmental status, although FLM is larger than two of the other three in the number of our majors, our budget, and the number of incoming freshmen that we attract each year.
The Department of Writing and Rhetoric has 42 majors, while the Department of Journalism has 88 majors [data for Fall 2021 semester].

Film/Media, serving 224 majors this Fall, is not given parity with these other units, which presents an unclear, confusing, and lopsided picture of the emphasis, resource allocation, and focus of the Harrington School and its aims, goals and the importance of its students within the overall structure.
This inequity sends a message to prospective and current students and their families that Film/Media may be less important and less vital than the rest of the Harrington School, and that it might not be the recipient of the attention and resources that a future major might desire.
The data on Film/Media emphasizes the contribution which is made by the major: FLM delivered 2,954 credit hours/semester (Fall 2019 CDR), a 14% increase over the prior year, and delivers approximately 900 General Education seats for the University each year.

5 We have participated in delivering a 3-credit version of FLM 101, FLM 100 for Accelerated Online Programs, for the RN-BS program and have been delivering 150 GenEd seats to that program every year since the inception of RN-BS’ in 2016.
We are in the process of adding an additional 3-credit version at the 300-level of FLM 205, History of Film II, as a new GenEd offering to Online Programs, and plan to get this approved in Fall 2021.
FLM has historically had to function with an extremely small faculty (1.5 tenure-track and 3 full-time Lecturers--the most recent only hired in 2020) and has been granted a TT line only once in its history, in 2010.
The lack of departmental status has certainly contributed to the University’s lack of investment in our major, creating a cycle that only allows growth to a certain point before it becomes unsustainable.
Film/Media’s student: teacher ratio was 22.6 in 2019 [CDR] with only 3% of credit hours delivered by tenure-track faculty.

The message may be inadvertent, but the result is clear: When only 3% of our credit hours are allowing our majors to interact with our tenured faculty, it is, indeed, extremely difficult for FLM to maintain the excellence which is drawing our majors to us and the Harrington School in the first place.
With a major with so much potential to deliver in-demand skills in a time of unprecedented opportunity, innovation, and emphasis on this field, departmental status will help to break this cycle and encourage University interest, support, and the resources required for growth and the continued level of pedagogical and academic excellence necessary for the future of FLM.
It should be noted that even with a small faculty, Film/Media has made constant and consistent contributions to the College and the University that would expand with the recognition that this organizational change would provide.
We have an active Graduate Faculty that sits on numerous PhD Committees for the English Department.

Importantly, for the Harrington School, it is noteworthy that both Associate Directors of the Harrington School are Film/Media faculty: Justin Wyatt was housed 1/3 in FLM (and is now a member of the FLM Unlimited Joint faculty), and Harrington’s second Associate Director, Nicholas Corsano, is a full-time Lecturer in FLM.
In 2020, URI righty granted department status to both Africana Studies [9 majors] and Gender and Women’s Studies [30 majors], and Film/Media submitted supporting letters for both.
In these cases, there were numerous reasons to make these organizational changes, not least of which is the inherent necessity to clarify and emphasize the crucial importance of diversity, equity, and social justice in our academic community.
The granting of departmental status is also importantly reflected in the words of the GWS proposal stating that it is “a visible declaration at URI of the equal stature it accords all of its academic units.” The shift to departmental status for Film/Media is also a similarly necessary statement of organizational equity in the University and the Harrington School that

6 supports, celebrates and recognizes the academic, cultural and economic importance of this discipline.
Film/Media is an active and essential participant in the ongoing success, not only for the Harrington School, but for the University as a whole.
FLM remains an essential contributor in attracting students to URI and should serve as a desirable home for a future growing creative, diverse, and globally-oriented faculty.
It should be granted Departmental status-- and the validation, expectations and goals that accompany that change-- to not only reflect our students’ and faculty’s positions in the life of the University, but also the very essential role that Film/Media plays in promoting the unique blend of fostering creativity, advanced training in technical skills, and the career preparation for success for our students that the major is designed to deliver.

INSTITUTIONAL ROLE: The organizational change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution 1.

Explain how the organizational change is consistent with published role and mission of institution and how it is related to institutional planning.
The articulation of the transformational and essential goals and mission of the University which are presented in the statement of the Academic Strategic Plan emphasizes the overarching focus on “Innovation with Impact.” These three words could not more clearly also express a description of what the Film/Media major is designed to achieve, and the goals that we have set for the major, our students and our faculty.
These goals can best be reached by this organizational change to department status, to assure the recognition of these “innovations and impacts” that our faculty and students make to be recognized as products of a discipline that is appreciated and fully supported by the University community.
There can be no doubt that the visual moving image is-- and will remain-- at the forefront of communication in the arts, in business, and across emerging and existing social media in the 21st century.
Department Status will ensure that FLM can deliver the promise set out by the goals of our major, the Harrington School, and URI.

This overarching introduction to the University Academic Strategic Plan 2016-2021 emphasizes these three goals: ~~Exciting and relevant collaborations deeply rooted in innovation that push the frontiers of learning, discovery, and problem solving: Film/Media is an interdisciplinary major, encouraging students to seek to explore, examine, and “push the frontiers” of ways of thinking and integrating learning across majors. 45%

7 of FLM majors are double majors in disciplines across the Harrington School and as varied as Marine Affairs, Global Languages, Wildlife Conservation, and Innovation Management.
Our major is one that inherently defines and executes the General Education goal of “Integrate and Apply,” as our students bring their unique and varied array of wide resources and approaches to learning to our classrooms. ~~New applications of technology that promote innovation, engagement, efficiency and effectiveness: Film/Media is necessarily at the locus of new technologies of communication.

This does not just include cameras and visual recording equipment, but, of course, also emphasizes new software applications and breakthrough programming that will challenge and change the ways in which content for art, media, and business is created and produced in the future. ~~A community that reflects innovation and a commitment to strategic institutional advancement is all areas: Film/Media’s faculty and leadership have consistently been present and active in supporting new and ongoing initiatives at the University: we were among the first majors to create and submit new General Education courses at the inception of the new GenEd program in 2015; we supported the RN-BS program as it became operational with some of its first course offerings; we participated in offering special 1-credit courses for the University as the COVID crisis deepened.

FLM offers unique education/experiential learning opportunities like our annual trip to the South by Southwest Conference and Festival and JTerm experiences in Cape Verde and Belize; our faculty has developed and run alumni career panels and film screenings; and we connect the University with the community through our Client Media program which pairs FLM majors with local companies and non-profits to produce PSAs or advertisements.
The change to departmental status will afford FLM opportunities to expand these classroom learning and experiential opportunities in several ways: as a fully recognized department of the University--and an equal partner in the structural dynamics of the Harrington School--FLM should more strongly attract internship and mentoring opportunities from members of the Harrington Advisory Board and other corporate contacts; as a department, it is hoped that Film/Media will more easily expand its tenure- track faculty--and attract Joint Faculty from other URI departments-- both of which will increase and open dialogues about new ideas and original, interdisciplinary avenues.

The faculty of Film/Media sit on a variety of University Committees: the University Joint Steering Classroom Committee, the University Alumni and Family Weekend Committee, the Center for the Humanities, the Service & Community Life Committee, the Executive Committee of URI/AAUP, and have served as moderators for Student Entertainment Committee events.
Of course, the FLM faculty is also active in many areas of the Faculty

8 Senate.
On the College level, members of our faculty have served on the Arts & Sciences Curriculum Committee, the A&S Committee on Diversity, and a wide range of ongoing committee work for the Harington School.
Film/Media is an integral contributor--and highly visible member--of the academic and service communities at URI, and this should be reflected in granting the major Departmental status.
Most importantly, Film/Media directly addresses 4 of the major goals in the University Academic Strategic Plan 2016-2021: Goal #1: Enhance Student Success: Strategy #2: Significantly expand opportunities for experiential learning within all majors, and restructure academic advising and career advising to better support students in meeting their life goals~~ As mentioned above, Film/Media is consistently offering new and varied travel and experiential learning opportunities for our students.
Because of the nature of our major, we have many requests from national production companies, community organizations, businesses, and other departments across the University for the services of our students.

Our majors are expected to understand how to behave as professionals from the beginning of their careers with us, as teaching film is teaching a professional skill and a professional experience that encompasses not just the technical and creative aspects of film production, but, importantly, the ways in which our students learn the nature of teamwork and collaboration which is the underpinning of all visual media creation.
Film/Media advising emphasizes the very unique and individual nature of our majors as each of them approaches their interest in film through different avenues.
This is not only reflected in the wide variety of double majors that we see in FLM students, but this is also seen in the ways in which they choose to work, or concentrate, within the broad categories of film production: narrative film, documentary production, commercial/corporate work, and art or experimental cinemas.
We emphasize that each of our majors is on a unique path through our major and URI, and their career choices and goals--because the Film/TV industries offer so many different types of work---will be individualized.

Recognizing the nature of this means that Film/Media advisors are focused on enhancing the personal success of each student and appreciating the unique goals that we must help them reach.
Strategy #5: Reframe and redefine liberal education at URI in the context of the 21st century~~ The 21st century has “reframed and redefined” liberal education, and this statement of this strategy is reflective of the ways in which the University is committed as an active participant in these changes.
The Harrington School tagline of “Think.
Create.
Communicate” could not more aptly describe the process of filmmaking, the important

9 nature of collaboration on these projects, and the emphasis on both technical and critical analytical skills that are embodied in the FLM major. “Liberal Education” now often means to our students and their families a grounding in critical reading, critical writing, and critical thinking skills, that must be applied to critical and skillful communication that opens avenues to successful and rewarding careers.
These three tenets of the liberal education project are now, more than ever, being considered in light of hands-on technical and professional skills that our alumni can bring to the jobs they will encounter.
Film/Media is a major with the unique position of offering not only strong communication and analytical skills, but these strengths are added to a wide array of technical job-ready knowledge, aptitude, and experiences that mean that our majors graduate from the University with extremely concrete skills in hand.
Film/Media asks our majors to be flexible, open to new experiences and opportunities--as well as the unexpected--and always to embrace new ways of doing things.

Film, itself, for over 125 years, has always been at the forefront of cultural, sociological, and technological breakthroughs, and the major, as a department, should be a visible leader at URI in introducing, experimenting with, and solidifying new ways to teach and learn.
Goal #2: Expand Research, Scholarship, and Creative work Strategy #1: Broaden resources and support for significant growth in research opportunities with the state, nation, and world, and demonstrate value and recognition for multiple forms of scholarship~~ The FLM faculty has applied for and been awarded URI Project Completion Grants, Faculty Career Enhancement Grants, and grants from the Rhode Island State Council on the Arts.
Professor Justin Wyatt has just been awarded the Ralph C. and Mary Lynn Heid Research Fellowship, at the University of Michigan for his upcoming sabbatical research.
Professor Keith Brown was designated as a consultant for a Course Development Grant with Kathryn S.
Meier, Associate Director, Institute for Integrated Health and Innovation, Cancer Prevention Research Center and Justin Z.
Laferrier, Assistant Professor, Physical Therapy Department at URI.

The FLM faculty has participated yearly in proposals for Champlin grants, including awards for the $100,000 Phantom camera, the $1.25 million Broadcast Center renovations, and other innovative equipment proposals.
Because of the nature of their professional work, the film faculty, by definition, demonstrates “the value and recognition of multiple forms of scholarship.” We are critical and analytical scholars of film and television and other forms of visual media, participating in a wide range of scholarship over various topics relevant to the history, theory, and ongoing innovations of the moving image, the cultural and artistic impact of filmic artifacts, and the film, television, and media industries.
The faculty also embodies creative work and research in experimental, documentary, narrative, and corporate/commercial filmmaking.
As noted in Goal #3 below, this faculty research is global in nature and practice, consistently bringing our faculty work into the international arena.
Granting

10 departmental status for Film/Media is essential in recognizing the many scholarly, pedagogical, and creative contributions of this faculty, and will allow them more opportunity and visibility for their work to be reflected and foregrounded in the overall achievements of the Harrington School and the University.
Strategy #4: Involve undergraduate and graduate students in rich and varied research, creative projects and other opportunities~~ Film/Media continues to offer new and innovative courses and topics.
At the University’s request to create and deliver special 1-credit courses during AY21 to offset the negative impact of learning under COVID, Professor Keith Brown developed a course for the Harrington school, SCM 351X: Broadcasting Contemporary Issues.
This fully remote, online course allowed students to research, prepare and record broadcasting segments on their reflections on the many vital current issues going on during that difficult year.
Every week those segments were edited together to present a television show that was aired online.

This class was offered in Fall 2020 and Spring 2021 as a special 1-credit course experience and was so successful that it is being offered again for Fall 2021.
Professor Mary Healey Jamiel developed FLM 444: Filmmakers Professional Portfolio.
This course, which may serve as a prototype for the Harrington School, prepares the Film/Media major for entry into their chosen professional fields.
Offered beginning in Fall, 2020, this course asks students to prepare a portfolio reflective of their work at URI, including a PSA to be shot during this course, and to hone the skills necessary to present themselves and their work and launch successfully into professional careers.
Film/Media continues to offer a plethora of special events and opportunities for our students including end-of-the semester student film screenings-- attended by friends and families-- and a wide variety of guest speakers: industry professionals, alumni, and filmmakers with Q&A sessions for our majors.
In Fall 2019, we hosted director Spike Lee’s editor, Hey Mee Na, for an in- person discussion and Q&A for our students.

Even in the difficult AY21, Film/Media ran a YouTube series “URI Film Presents,” releasing weekly student work, and “Life After Harrington” presented a conversation between Professor Keith Brown and alumna, Ashton Avila about her burgeoning career in Los Angeles.
With the Harrington School, our majors participated in a media production talk with Victoria Coloruno-Caretto and Corrado Caretto.
Film/Media also invited the Hollywood film editor, Joaquin Elizondo, for an online talk and very impactful Q&A.
With great creativity, given COVID protocols, Professor Keith Brown arranged for the year- end film student screening in May, 2021 to be held at the Misquamicut Drive-In Theatre in Westerly, RI.
The event was a huge success and is reflective of the ways in which the FLM faculty constantly strives to offer our students--and the URI community-- new, original, and exciting events and experiences.
The annual trip to the South By Southwest Conference and Festival (SXSW) remains immensely popular to our majors and is fully enrolled every year.
This trip--which is

11 constructed as a full course--involves weeks of preparation ahead of the festival, participation in a plethora of events and screenings during this important festival, and follow-up work and analysis on the students’ return to campus.
Film/Media also joined forces with Writing and Rhetoric to offer “Careers in Film and Writing Alumni Panel” at the Harrington School Job Fair, and we regularly offer the Client Media Independent Study for 5-10 students to be paired with local businesses and non-profits to produce film and video content.
In the classroom, our topics courses open up ever-changing concentrations on varying aspects of the study of the moving image.
Each of these new topics then encourages students to consider new research and new avenues of thought.

In AY20 and AY 21, some of these topics included: FLM 220: Making Personal Media, Introduction to Cinematography, Introduction to Directing, and Creative Cloud Workshop; FLM 351: Producing the Short Narrative Film, Analog Cinematography, and Advanced Cinematography; FLM 352: American Independent Cinema, Animated Television, True Crime in Film and TV; FLM 451: International Animated Film, British Comedy Film, and International Long-Form Television; FLM 495: Global Art Cinema.
The recognition of Film/Media as a department will introduce resources and recognition for the major to expand these innovative offerings that so richly supplement the academic careers of students in FLM, the Harrington School and URI, and will attract both internal and external partners to develop new potential curriculum initiatives.

Goal #3: Grow a Global Presence: Strategy #3: Create opportunities for the internationalization of the curriculum and co- curriculum to ensure that all students are exposed to global perspectives and build global competence~~ Film/Media holds an essentially central focus in delivering global and international content to our students, and we emphasize the importance of global content in our curriculum in many ways.
One of the foundational aspects of our teaching is that all critical studies courses, including FLM 101, should contain at least 50% international or global films on our syllabi.
Teaching film and TV means that we are focused on global media and on instilling in our students a true understanding of different global perspectives, cultural attitudes, and the ways in which lives, people, and places occupy their spaces in the world and how that relates to our students here in Rhode Island.
Film is a global industry, and the viewing and production of film is usually not defined by geopolitical borders or demarcations.

The Film/Media major is one that must--and does-- always forefront the world in which the film artifact moves and exists, the populations that consume and view it, and the essential importance to our students of understanding the global impact and interconnectivity of what they watch and create.

12 Strategy #4: Create institutional policies and support mechanisms to provide faculty with opportunities to develop global competence to maximize the impact of student global experiences on learning outcomes~~ Film/Media faculty maintain a solid international presence: in the past several years, we have represented the discipline at conferences in London and Scotland.
Films by our faculty have been shown in Germany, India, Lithuania, Dubai, Lebanon, and The Netherlands.
Professor Mary Healey Jamiel’s film, Searchdog , was released on iTunes internationally in the UK, Canada, and Ireland.
Professor Ashish Chadha’s body of work is streaming on MUBI’s platform for art cinema with 10 million subscribers in over 195 territories around the world.
Professor Chadha’s significant accomplishment and presence as a world-renowned filmmaker underlines the ways in which he operates at the highest level of the art of filmmaking, reinventing and reimagining the limits of the form to create and express work in an innovative and provocative manner.

Film/Media faculty demonstrate a total commitment to the advancement of their craft, with an impressive record of creative work screened/broadcast around the globe.
Faculty work is consistently selected for important festivals, national/international broadcasts, theatrical screenings and college and museum lectures.
Film/Media is dedicated to supporting our faculty in their creative work and research and in assuring that this work is seen and applauded internationally.
Our faculty’s wide and ongoing experiences in engaging with geopolitical spaces around the globe, and the wide scope of Film/Media’s international visibility, warrants Departmental recognition for our faculty’s continued contribution to URI’s and the Harrington School’s global footprint.
Goal #4: Embrace Diversity and Social Justice Strategy #2: Increase the recruitment, retention, and graduation of students from underrepresented groups, and provide support for their inclusion and success in the academic environment~~ The Film/Media major is dedicated to Diversity and Social Justice.

This is, of course, reflected in our curriculum as we focus on films and filmmakers that we study from every geography and nation, from all ethnicities, gender identities, and sexual orientations.
As a discipline that is enmeshed in inter-and multi-disciplinary studies, the foundation of FLM relies on --and focuses upon--exposure to different voices and different ways of seeing.
Film/Media is defined by the concept that film and filmmaking is universal, humanistic, and that the making and appreciation of art--and its inclusion in our lives-- is, perhaps, one of the foremost common denominators of the shared human experience.
Recruitment: Film/Media--with the support of the Harrington School-- has pursued for several years the possibility of introducing a program of concurrent enrollment between URI and the JM Walsh School for the Visual and Performing Arts in Pawtucket, RI, so that students at JM Walsh will receive college credit while finishing high school.
This successful

13 proposal allows for the offering of three courses required for the FLM major: FLM 101, 110 and 220 to be taught at JM Walsh to students in their Junior and Senior High School years.
This is an extremely positive step in opening up avenues for diverse students to enter the University with some coursework completed and a foothold into the FLM major.
Beginning in Spring, 2022, our first FLM courses will be held at the JM Walsh school, and we are very much looking forward to working closely with the school to support this curriculum with on-campus events and screenings, and collaborative interactions with our majors.
JM Walsh also offers majors in Art, Music and Theater, and we are hoping that this program will introduce students to the wider Harrington School disciplines and other URI majors as well.
In addition, to aid in recruitment and retention, since 2018, Film/Media has offered FLM 100 and FLM 110 in tandem as part of the summer Talent Development Program (we did not offer this in Summer 2020 because of the difficulties of teaching introductory production remotely during COVID).

Successful recruitment of diverse students will remain problematic without the organizational change for FLM to department status.
Although it is difficult to quantify, it can be assumed that prospective students and families may well be uncertain about committing to a major that is allocated only as a program, and that concern no doubt stems from questions of resource allocations and available institutional support for the major and its students.
In addition, it is no doubt more difficult for our Admissions Office to advocate on behalf of a discipline that has somehow not seen and named as a department.
It is extremely important for FLM to become a department in order to better attract our major to potential students of all backgrounds.
Department status conferred on Film/Media will also strengthen our ability to engage with the community, as we have with JM Walsh and encourage them to participate in often difficult negotiations to institute new and innovative programs.
Inclusion/Retention: Film/Media is committed to diversity, inclusivity and anti-racist principles.

Our topics courses focus on an extensive variety of film from differing geopolitical areas, among filmmakers around the globe, and which address difficult and relevant topics concerning race, gender, economic and social disparities, and the history and ongoing reality of oppression, power, and imperial violence.
Filmmaking affords all of our students a voice, and our end-of-semester student film screenings, which are attended by friends and families and other URI students and community members, assure that every student’s work is seen and heard.
We encourage our students to submit their work to film festivals, and, with the support of the Harrington School and the College of Arts & Sciences as well, Film/Media has been able to help students to attend important and prestigious festival screenings of their films.
We also are able to offer our students paid work in the Ranger Hall Media Equipment Center and as Student Assistants to Film/Media.
All available scholarships are awarded based on need.
The ethos of Film/Media is to form a cohesive working, creative and

14 inquiring community--and the center of that is the foundational practice of the importance, equality, opportunity, and dignity of every member of our community.
Strategy #3: Create an active learning community among students, faculty, staff, and administrators that engages in open discourse and enhance understanding about what it means to be a diverse and socially just community.
As an interdisciplinary major, FLM offers courses from Africana Studies and Gender and Women’s Studies, including the cross-listed ENG/AAF 352, Black Images in Film.
Studies in French, Italian and Spanish cinemas also count towards completion of the major, and have focused on Hispanic, Carribean, LatinX, and Maghreb filmmakers.
In the Fall of 2020, FLM faculty joined in a co-teaching project with Professors from Theatre and Honors to offer a section of AAF 300: Challenging Racism Through Film and Theatre.
This special topic course investigated the relation between race and theatre, and how racial issues have impacted on, or have, in turn, been affected by theatrical/filmic representations of race.
We are certainly hoping to offer this course again in the future.

Part of the gift of the FLM major is the ways in which our students work collaboratively on each other's films from beginning to end, and learn so much about each other in this process, as well as about the situations and topics around which their films are based.
Our diverse students are often tackling very personal subjects and reflecting on their histories and their lives in ways that intimately open up realities and lived experiences to other students.
Filmmaking--and discussions about the films that we watch and analyze together--is often difficult, as film leaves no topic unopened and ultimately excludes no one from the conversation, and Film/Media assures our commitment to that goal.
Film/Media has a small, but diverse faculty.
Our hope is to maintain equitable representation in not only the films that we include on our syllabi, but in promoting the ways in which the production of the moving image is not only a locus of international and global realities and creative endeavors, but a discipline that must ensure that all voices are heard and that all voices are afforded the opportunity to speak and be seen.

Our current position request for a potential future hire asks for an Assistant Professor of Production & Post-Production, specifically with a record of work that addresses issues of race, social and/or economic inequity and social justice.
Creating a Department of Film/Media should afford us a stronger chance of having this hire--and future diverse hires-- funded.
It is a goal of FLM to not only forefront the moving image as a reflection and focus of international and global realities and creative endeavors, but to also ensure that we are a part of the project that actively ensures that the film/TV and media industries move constantly towards social justice, equity, and diversity.

As an interdisciplinary major, Film/Media’s history has emphasized--and proven-- its dedication to multi- and inter-disciplinary cooperation and collaboration.
Department status will strengthen Film/Media’s impact and contributions to the academic disciplines and units among whom we have long worked.
Very importantly, the change to Department status for Film/Media will have a highly positive impact on the Harrington School, as it will strengthen its position as a fully formed school of communication with departments of equal value, importance, and strength.

The appearance that Film/Media is somehow minimized in comparison to the other units in Harrington will be corrected, and this will greatly influence the Harrington School’s ability to recruit, support, and retain students who are eager to major or second major in the very important field of visual media production.
Because the skills in Film/Media so importantly overlap with those of the other Harrington units — and particularly with the new Sports Media major-- it is essential for the Harrington School to present a balanced structure of its majors.
As a department, Film/Media will more confidently plan future contributions to the Harrington School and the University including potential interdisciplinary minors like Television Studies/Production, the development of multi-interdisciplinary General Education courses—especially in Grand Challenge, for example with collaborations with THE on Costuming, Set Design, or Performance in Film-- and investigating opportunities for co-teaching and team teaching of multi- and inter-disciplinary courses.

As the goals of the Harrington School state, granting Film/Media departmental status will serve to support, “accelerate and extend faculty and student engagement and collaboration in innovative, high-impact, and multidisciplinary teaching and research.” D.
